client: I've been really dreading this family reunion that's coming up next month, and honestly it's been keeping me up at night. My cousin has this habit of making comments about my career in front of everyone, like pointing out that I'm not making enough money or that I chose the wrong path, and it just makes me feel so humiliated. I'm not even sure talking about it will change anything, because the reunion is still going to happen and my cousin isn't going to suddenly become a different person.
therapist: What you're describing sounds genuinely painful — being publicly criticized by someone you're supposed to feel safe around is a real source of shame and dread, and it makes complete sense that it's disrupting your sleep. I also notice that even as you're sharing this, there's a lot of energy and intensity in how you're talking about it, which makes me wonder if part of you is actually quite angry about how your cousin treats you, even if it's hard to name it that way. While we can't change your cousin, I'd love to explore what *you* might have more control over — whether that's how you prepare yourself mentally, how you respond in the moment, or even what story you tell yourself about your worth when those comments land.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, loud, fast speech

client: Yeah, I guess angry is the right word, even though I've been trying to convince myself I'm just stressed. It feels almost shameful to admit that, like I should be above letting my cousin get to me this much. But honestly, the part about controlling my own response — I don't know, it sounds good in theory, but in the moment I just kind of freeze and go along with it, and I can't imagine that changing just because I thought about it beforehand.
therapist: It's really brave to name the anger, and I want to gently push back on the idea that feeling it means you've somehow failed — being hurt and angry when someone repeatedly humiliates you isn't a weakness, it's a very human response. The freezing you describe in those moments is actually incredibly common, and it doesn't mean change is impossible — it usually means your nervous system is protecting you before your conscious mind can catch up. What if we explored what a small, manageable response might look like in those moments — not a perfect comeback, but just something tiny that helps you feel a little less like you disappeared?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I like the idea of something small, but I'm already second-guessing myself because even a tiny response feels risky — like if I say anything at all, it might escalate things or make the whole reunion awkward for everyone else. There's also this part of me that worries if I respond differently this time, people will think I'm being dramatic or oversensitive, since I've just kind of laughed it off before. So I guess I'm not sure what "small" even looks like when the stakes feel so high in my head.
therapist: The way you're talking about this — weighing everyone else's comfort so carefully, worrying about being seen as dramatic — makes me wonder if one of the hardest parts isn't actually your cousin at all, but this deep fear of taking up space and having your own needs matter in that room. That belief that protecting the group's comfort is more important than protecting yourself from repeated humiliation is worth gently examining, because it might be the very thing that keeps you frozen. What do you think it would mean about you if you *did* respond, and someone felt uncomfortable — whose voice in your head decides that would be your fault?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That question actually stopped me for a second, because I think the voice is my mom's — she always made it really clear that keeping the peace was the most important thing, and that stirring things up was selfish. So if someone got uncomfortable because of something I said, I think it would mean I was being a troublemaker, that I was the problem. It's weird to hear it out loud because part of me knows that's not totally fair, but it still feels completely true at the same time.
therapist: What you just uncovered is really significant — that "troublemaker" label wasn't something you chose for yourself, it was handed to you, and it's been quietly running the show ever since. It's so common to hold two truths at once like you're describing: the part that *knows* it isn't fair, and the part that *feels* it as absolute — and that gap between knowing and feeling is actually exactly where the work happens. I'm curious, when you imagine a version of you who sets a small boundary at that reunion and someone does feel briefly uncomfortable — what's the worst thing that version of you would have to accept about herself?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: I think the worst thing would be accepting that I'm someone who causes problems, that I'm not the easy, agreeable person everyone expects me to be. And honestly, that feels like losing something — like if I stop being the one who keeps the peace, I don't know who I am in that family anymore. It's strange because I came in here thinking this was about my cousin, and now it feels like it's about something much bigger and scarier than just one reunion.
therapist: What you just said — that you don't know who you are in that family without the peacekeeper role — that's one of the most honest and courageous things a person can recognize about themselves, and it makes complete sense that it feels bigger and scarier than the reunion. That role probably kept you safe for a long time, so grieving it is real, even as you start to question whether it's still serving you. I want you to know that discovering who you are *beyond* that role isn't losing yourself — it might actually be the beginning of finding yourself.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I hear what you're saying, and part of me wants to believe it, but "finding yourself" sounds like something that takes a long time — and the reunion is in a month. I'm also a little scared that if I start pulling at this thread, I'm going to show up there feeling even more unsettled than I would have otherwise, like I've opened something up without having time to put it back together. I guess I'm wondering if there's a way to work on this without feeling like I'm walking into that room as a half-finished version of myself.
therapist: That fear of walking in half-assembled is so understandable, and I want to reassure you that the goal for the next month isn't to resolve everything — it's just to give you one or two steady things to hold onto in that room. You haven't opened something up to break yourself down; you've started to see the pattern clearly, and that clarity can actually be a quiet source of strength, even when the deeper work is still unfolding. What if we focused next on something concrete and grounding — like identifying one simple thing you can say to yourself *in the moment* when your cousin makes a comment, something that reminds you of what you now know about where that freeze comes from?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: Okay, I think I can try that — having something internal feels less risky than actually saying something out loud to my cousin. But I'm struggling to think of what that phrase would even be, because in the moment everything goes blank and whatever I'd planned feels completely out of reach. Can you help me figure out what it might sound like, because I honestly don't trust myself to come up with something that would actually work when I'm that activated?
therapist: The way you're asking for help here — a little quietly, like you're not sure you deserve to get it right — makes me want to gently reflect that back, because trusting yourself is actually part of what we're building toward, not a prerequisite for starting. A phrase that tends to work well in those activated moments is something short and grounding that reconnects you to your own perspective, like *"This is about their stuff, not my worth"* — simple enough that it can surface even when your mind goes blank. Does something like that resonate, or does it need to sound more like *your* voice for it to feel real in that moment?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech

client: That phrase actually does resonate a little, but I think I'd need it to feel more automatic, like something I've said to myself enough times that it doesn't feel like a script. The version that sounds more like me might be something like "this is his thing, not mine" — shorter, more specific to him. But I'm already imagining being at that table and hearing him say something, and I'm not sure even a phrase I love is going to cut through the noise in my head in that moment.
therapist: "This is his thing, not mine" is perfect — it's yours, it's specific, and that matters enormously for it to actually land in a high-stress moment. The way you're already rehearsing that table scene in your mind is actually something we can use, because the more you practice the phrase *while* imagining that moment — not just in calm reflection — the more your nervous system starts to recognize it as a real option when things get loud. Would you be willing to try sitting with that image this week, letting yourself feel a little of the discomfort, and then quietly offering yourself that phrase — almost like building a small muscle you'll need next month?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I'm willing to try it, but I have to be honest — deliberately sitting with that uncomfortable image sounds kind of awful, and I'm not sure I won't just avoid it all week because it feels bad. I think my instinct will be to distract myself the moment it starts to feel real, which is probably exactly the problem. Is there a way to make it feel less like I'm just torturing myself and more like I'm actually doing something useful?
therapist: The honesty in what you just said — naming the avoidance impulse *before* it even happens — is actually a really sophisticated form of self-awareness, and it's worth recognizing that you're not describing a flaw, you're describing exactly how humans are wired to protect themselves from discomfort. We can make this feel less like torture by shrinking it way down — instead of sitting with the full scene, what if you just held the phrase "this is his thing, not mine" for thirty seconds each morning this week, without needing to conjure the table or your cousin at all, just letting it become familiar in your mouth and your mind? The goal isn't to suffer through the fear — it's just to make that phrase feel like yours before you need it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: Thirty seconds does sound manageable, and I think I could actually do that without talking myself out of it. But I'm a little worried that if I just say it in the quiet of my morning routine, it's going to feel too disconnected from the actual situation — like I'll have this phrase that feels fine at home and then completely useless when I'm sitting across from him and my stomach is in knots. I guess I just don't fully trust yet that something that small can actually make a difference when everything feels so big in that moment.
therapist: The doubt you're describing is completely valid, and it actually points to something important — you're right that calm practice and real stress are different experiences, so let's bridge that gap a little. Once the phrase feels familiar after a few mornings, you could try saying it at a moment during the week when you're *mildly* stressed — not the full reunion scene, but maybe when something smaller frustrates you — so it starts to build a connection to activated feelings, not just quiet ones. Small things can carry real weight when they've been practiced enough to become instinct, and you're already doing the hardest part by staying with this instead of walking away.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, fast speech
